references.text: Earlier in the same chapter it is stated that the manslayer must remain in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest, which is the same provision repeated here.
The introduction of the cities of refuge as a place for the manslayer to flee to.
Prohibits accepting ransom money to allow the manslayer to return before the death of the high priest.
Joshua repeats the law concerning the cities of refuge and that the manslayer must stay there until the death of the high priest.
Hebron is designated as a city of refuge for manslayers, a practical application of the law.
The book of Hebrews uses the image of refuge to describe believers fleeing to Christ for salvation, a typological fulfillment of the cities of refuge.
Christ as the great high priest whose death brings eternal redemption, a typological parallel to the death of the high priest that releases the manslayer.
